key_takeaways: Health spending reached 12.27 percent of GDP in 2024, up from 10.59 percent in 2012; only the US spends more.{{health_system.financing:1}}{{health_system.financing:6}}
Public sources paid 86 percent of health spending in 2023, against an EU average of 80 percent.{{health_system.financing:5}}
The 2026 stabilization law answers a saving need of almost €19 billion (US$21.3 billion) for 2027.{{health_system.outlook:2}}{{health_system.outlook:3}}
The 65 and over share is projected to reach 28 percent by 2050; 49 percent have multiple chronic conditions.{{health_system.outlook:1}}
health_system: Insurance is mandatory: an estimated 89.0 percent of residents had statutory cover in 2024, and 10.4 percent had private cover.{{health_system.public_system:1}}
Germany had the EU's highest rate of avoidable hospital admissions for chronic conditions in 2023, at 810 per 100,000 people.{{health_system.public_system:1}}
The 16 Länder plan hospitals, and reform adjustments delay full fixed capacity payments until 2030.{{country_overview.government:5}}{{health_system.outlook:5}}
market: In 2025 Germany had 1,807 hospitals: 729 private, 549 nonprofit and 529 public.{{health_system.private_system:1}}

Helios, Asklepios and Sana lead by beds; Swiss-based Ameos and Turkey's Medicana took over hospitals in 2026.{{health_system.competitive_landscape:1}}{{health_system.competitive_landscape:5}}{{health_system.competitive_landscape:6}}
About 182,200 patients from abroad were treated in 2022, three quarters from neighboring countries.{{health_system.competitive_landscape:4}}
risks: Statutory insurance finances remain tense, and structural problems must still be solved, the health minister said.{{health_system.outlook:4}}
Growth is weak: GDP grew 0.2 percent in 2025, and the Bundesbank projects 0.5 percent for 2026.{{country_overview.economy:3}}{{country_overview.economy:6}}
Almost a quarter (23.4 percent) of working doctors were 60 or older in 2025.{{health_system.workforce:1}}

recent.text: Estimators expect the average additional contribution to stay at 2.9 percent in 2027, and Minister Linnemann called the situation tense.{{recent_developments.4:1}}
Carsten Linnemann replaced Nina Warken as federal health minister, and Warken moved to head the Chancellery.{{recent_developments.3:4}}{{recent_developments.3:1}}
Parliament passed the contribution stabilization law, in force from 30 July, tying spending growth to income growth.{{recent_developments.2:1}}{{recent_developments.2:2}}

country_background: Germany, a federal parliamentary republic of 16 Länder, has its capital in Berlin and had about 83.5 million residents at the end of 2025.{{country_overview.demographics:3}} Federal President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is head of state, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz leads a CDU/CSU and SPD coalition.{{country_overview.demographics:7}}{{country_overview.government:3}} Carsten Linnemann became federal health minister on 29 July 2026.{{country_overview.government:9}} GDP was about 6.30 trillion international dollars (PPP) in 2025, or about 75,400 per person, after 0.2 percent real growth.{{country_overview.economy:1}}{{country_overview.economy:2}}{{country_overview.economy:3}} The population is aging: 23.7 percent were 65 or older in 2025, and life expectancy was 81.5 years in 2024.{{country_overview.demographics:13}}{{country_overview.demographics:12}} The main risk is financial: the 2026 stabilization law answers a needed saving of almost €19 billion (US$21.3 billion) for 2027.{{health_system.outlook:2}}
